data.title: Nationwide recall on these compound GLP-1 drugs
data.description:
(NewsNation) — The FDA has issued a recall for 23 GLP-1 compounded vials from Apothecary Pharma LLC due to lack of assurance the vials are sterile.

The FDA has designated the recall as Class II, meaning exposure to the products could cause reversible or temporary health consequences and poses little risk of serious consequences from use, according to the FDA website.

What products to look out for:

The recall applies to 22 vials of Tirzepatide Injection, 18mg/mL, 4 mL Sterile Multi-Dose Vial, Rx only, Apothecary Pharma, LLC, 1913 Evans Road, Cary, NC 27513, NDC 85091-001-18. Tirzepatide is used in Zepbound and Mounjaro. Customers should look out for these specific codes:

  • Lot AP-202622, BUD 07-Oct-2026
  • Lot AP-202623, BUD 08-Oct-2026
  • Lot AP-202624, BUD 19-Oct-2026
  • Lot AP-202625, BUD 10/20/2026
  • Lot AP-202627, BUD 10/26/2026
  • Lot AP-202628, BUD 10/27/2026
  • Lot AP-202629, BUD 10/28/2026
  • Lot AP-202630, BUD 10/31/2026
  • Lot AP-202631, BUD 11/01/2026
  • Lot AP-202632, BUD 11/03/2026
  • Lot AP-202633, BUD 11/07/2026
  • Lot AP-202634, BUD 11/08/2026
  • Lot AP-202635, BUD 11/16/2026
  • Lot AP-202636, BUD 11/17/2026
  • Lot AP-202637,BUD 11/18/2026
  • Lot AP-202638, BUD 11/19/2026
  • Lot AP-202639, BUD 11/20/2026
  • Lot AP-202640, BUD 11/21/2026
  • Lot AP-202641, BUD 11/22/2026
  • Lot AP-202642, BUD 11/24/2026
  • Lot AP-202643, BUD 11/25/2026
  • Lot AP-202644, BUD 11/26/2026

The recall also applies to one vial of NAD+ Injection 200 mg/mL, 6 mL Sterile Multi-Dose Vial, Rx Only, Apothecary Pharma, LLC, 1913 Evans Road, Cary, NC, 27513, NDC 85091-011-06. The code information is: Lot #: AP-202647, BUD 13-Oct-2026

Compounding pharmacy flagged by the FDA before

Apothecary Pharma in December 2025 received a letter from the FDA stating, “FDA investigators noted that drug products intended or expected to be sterile were prepared, packed, or held under insanitary conditions, whereby they may have become contaminated with filth or rendered injurious to health, causing your drug products to be adulterated under section 501(a)(2)(A) of the FDCA.”

What are compounding pharmacies?

Apothecary Pharma LLC is a compounding pharmacy in North Carolina. Compounded GLP-1s are not FDA-approved or name-brand. These pharmacies create customized versions of drugs for patients rather than mass-producing them like a commercial pharmacy, and they can adjust medications and create new versions to meet the patient’s specific needs

Although these pharmacies use FDA-approved ingredients, the products themselves are not checked for effectiveness, safety or purity, according to an article in Harvard Health Publishing. The FDA occasionally grants these pharmacies permission to produce drugs in bulk during shortages. In 2022, compounders were given permission to produce their own GLP-1 drugs to fill a shortage at the time. However, tirzepatide and semaglutide were removed from the drug shortage list in late 2024 and early 2025, according to Pharmacy Times reporting. Compound pharmacies continue to produce GLP-1s despite the lack of a shortage.

The FDA has not released official instructions on what to do if you discover you purchased a recalled vial; no illnesses have been linked to the recall at this time. Consumers should stop using it and contact their healthcare provider for guidance.

data.title: Vance becomes a hurricane as it nears Mexico
data.description:
Hurricane Vance is expected to steadily intensify in the next 24 hours and turn into a major hurricane by Friday night, according to the projections of the National Hurricane Center.

“Swells generated by Vance are expected to begin affecting portions of the coast of southern and southwestern Mexico this weekend and continue into next week,” the hurricane center said in an advisory Friday morning.

“These swells are likely to cause life-threatening surf and rip current conditions,” the advisory said.

Vance, which became a hurricane Friday, was a Category 1 hurricane with maximum sustained winds of 90 mph and could become a major Category 3 hurricane before the end of Friday, the Associated Press reported.

It could be the seventh major hurricane in a row this year in the Pacific Ocean, following Nolo, Odalys, Polo, Rachel, Simon and Trudy.

The northeastern and central Pacific basins saw a number of powerful storms this year with at least 20 named storms in the region by Sept. 28, according to a NASA report. Nine of those storms had reached hurricane strength.

The intense hurricane season in the Pacific comes as El Nino conditions create unusual weather patterns.

In July, the AP reported that this year’s El Nino had an 81 percent chance of becoming “very strong” by fall, altering weather patterns across the globe.

data.title: Appeals court rules Trump unlawfully deployed National Guard to California
data.description:
A federal appeals court on Friday ruled 2-1 that President Trump’s National Guard deployment to the Los Angeles area last year was unlawful. 

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit rejected Trump’s assertion that violent demonstrations in the city protesting his immigration crackdown justified him to wrest control of the troops from Gov. Gavin Newsom (D). 

Though Trump’s deployment has ended, the decision caps a year of consideration by the appeals court. 

At an earlier stage of the case, the 9th Circuit sided with Trump. It’s now ruling against him after the Supreme Court similarly found Trump didn’t meet the legal requirements to unilaterally deploy the National Guard to Chicago.

“Defendants have not made either of the required threshold showings here. Thus, they have not carried their burden,” U.S. Circuit Judge Jennifer Sung, an appointee of former President Biden. 

Sung was joined on the panel by two Trump-nominated judges, Eric Miller and Mark Bennett. Miller also sided against Trump, while Bennett dissented. 

Bennett said his colleagues shouldn’t have decided the case, as the administration wanted to dismiss the appeal and head back to the trial court to litigate the impact of the Supreme Court’s ruling.  

“But the majority insists on pressing forward, relying primarily on outdated briefs prepared amid a shifting legal landscape,” Bennett wrote. 

It means Friday’s decision will now bind future 9th Circuit panels if Trump tries to deploy the National Guard again in California. 

Last year, Trump deployed the National Guard to various blue cities around the country — including Washington, D.C., Memphis and Portland, Ore. — to quell protests against his immigration crackdown.  

In Los Angeles, the demonstrations devolved into violence at times, with reports of looting and some having thrown Molotov cocktails.

The president deployed the National Guard by invoking a law allowing him to federalize troops whenever there is a rebellion or when he cannot execute the law with regular forces. 

The Supreme Court last year said Trump hadn’t met the criteria because “regular forces” likely refers to the U.S. military.

Trump’s National Guard deployment in the nation’s capital, which relies on a different legal authority, remains ongoing.

data.title: Meghan Markle says she's 'deeply distressed' in response to child pornography allegations against her father
data.description:
Meghan Markle has addressed the accusations against her father, who is being investigated over alleged possession of child sexual abuse material.

Markle, Duchess of Sussex and wife to Great Britain’s Prince Harry, said she was “deeply distressed” by the news on 82-year-old Thomas Markle Sr. that has spread through tabloids in recent days. Markle and her family recently returned to England after forfeiting their royal duties and living in the United States for a number of years.

“I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed,” Markle wrote in a statement obtained by The Hill. 

According to British tabloid The Sun, Markle’s half-brother Thomas Markle Jr. told police he found “hundreds if not thousands” of child sexual abuse images in his father’s home. Markle, who is said to be estranged from her father for years, said allegations were made to British police in 2018 and were later shared with her. 

“In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan Police and Royalty and Specialist Protection,” Markle wrote. “That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated.”

The Sun reported that Markle Jr. reported his father to officials after finding the boxes of photos and a 15-minute video of naked young girls on his father’s phone. Markle Jr. reported his father to multiple law enforcement authorities, including the FBI, The Sun reported. 

The Duchess said in her statement that she trusted the authorities to protect any families at risk while she avoided her father to protect her young children.

“I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them,” Markle wrote. “I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families.”

Markle said she hopes that justice will be served and children will be protected.

“Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children,” Markle wrote.

data.title: Ex-FBI officials charged with lying to Congress about Hunter Biden probe
data.description:
Two former Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) officials are facing charges for lying to Congress about their involvement in the agency’s investigation into Hunter Biden’s laptop.

Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, who worked in FBI’s Foreign Influence Task Force (FITF) in 2019 and 2020, were taken into custody Friday, said FBI Director Kash Patel in a post on the social platform X.

Patel said in his post that both Floris and Benavides testified earlier that the FITF was not involved in the investigations into Biden, but documentary evidence, communications and witness accounts contradict their testimony.

“Lying to Congress by senior FBI officials strikes at the heart of our system,” Patel said. “No one is above the law.”

Biden’s laptop was seized by the FBI in 2019 and contained some of his personal information. The contents of the laptop, including emails showing discussions of Biden’s foreign business dealings, were published by the New York Post, which said it had obtained a hard drive of a computer dropped off by Biden at a Delaware repair shop, according to the Associated Press.

In a Friday release, the Department of Justice (DOJ) said the charges stem from an ongoing investigation into the FTIF.

The department cited evidence that Floris discussed the FBI’s investigations routinely for more than a year within the FITF and with others in the FBI. Benavides also regularly discussed the laptop investigation with FBI officials.

“The weaponization of government goes against the interest of the American people, and public servants, including federal law enforcement officials, cannot lie to Congress and get away with it,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said in the DOJ release.

Both Floris and Benavides made their first appearance in federal court in Washington following their surrender Friday, where their lawyers asked for a speedy hearing at which they could contest the allegations, the AP reported.

Floris’s lawyers issued a statement disputing the allegations and calling her “a patriot.”

“Nikki Floris is a patriot. She served our nation as a dedicated FBI intelligence officer for nearly 20 years,” a statement obtained by The Hill said.

“Yet today, the DOJ has accused her falsely of a crime on the say-so of politicians, not on the facts. It’s no coincidence the government is filing these nonsense charges now, years later, on the eve of an election,” the statement continued.

data.title: Watch live: Trump rallies in Fort Myers, Florida
data.description:
President Trump will rally in Fort Myers, Florida, on Friday as Republicans in the state are feeling bullish about statewide races.

Fort Myers is part of the 19th congressional district, where Rep. Byron Donalds (R) vacated his seat to run for governor. Donalds is favored to win against Democrat David Jolly in the race to replace term-limited Gov. Ron DeSantis (R), while Republican Jim Schwartzel is a heavy favorite to beat Democrat Victor Arias to fill Donalds’s seat.

Sen. Ashley Moody (R) is also leading in polls against Democrat Angie Nixon in her first election, after being tapped by DeSantis to replace Marco Rubio when he became secretary of state.

Florida’s 19th fits into a trend of Trump visiting safe red districts during his final midterm blitz, with the GOP facing stiff headwinds in battleground states across the country.

Trump is scheduled to speak at Friday’s rally at 2 p.m.

data.title: Put the last cell tower in orbit
data.description:
In a recent report, the Federal Communications Commission revealed a worrisome paradox in America’s cellular networks: they reach nearly everyone, but not nearly everywhere. While 95 percent of the U.S. population can receive 5G service from at least one carrier, only 69 percent of the nation’s road miles and 39 percent of its land area have such coverage. In rural America, the numbers fall to 60 percent and 38 percent.

This is the rural-mobile divide. It is not about whether a household can obtain broadband at home. It is about losing mobile service while driving, farming, hiking, fighting a wildfire or responding to an emergency.

The conventional solution is to build more cell towers. Some are still needed. But extending terrestrial networks to every remote road, ravine and mountaintop would be economically irrational. The FCC has approved a plan to provide up to $9 billion to close the remaining gaps in America’s 5G cellular networks. But instead of treating every dead zone as a construction problem, we should consider whether the last cell towers should instead be placed in orbit.

Technology advances now offer a promising alternative to cover this last and most expensive frontier. Direct-to-device satellite service allows an ordinary compatible cellphone to connect directly to a satellite when no terrestrial tower is available. The satellite effectively becomes a cell tower in space. No satellite phone, dish or other specialized equipment is required.

All three national carriers see satellites becoming an integral part of mobile networks. T-Mobile already offers this service through Starlink. The service is included with some T-Mobile plans and sold for $10 a month per line to other eligible users, including subscribers of competing carriers. AT&T and Verizon have their own satellite partnerships. And in May, all three carriers announced plans for a joint venture to expand direct-to-device coverage, pool spectrum and make it easier for satellite operators to reach their customers.

Direct-to-device satellite service doesn’t replace terrestrial 5G. Its capacity is limited, and initial offerings emphasize messaging, emergency communications and selected low-bandwidth applications. Voice and more capable data services are in development. But even basic connectivity can transform a dead zone into a place where someone can summon help, report an accident or tell family members they are safe.

The question is how to deploy that capability quickly and affordably. The answer begins with the FCC’s 5G Fund for Rural America. Subsidizing cellular services in areas where private investment alone won’t support deployment was originally proposed in the 2010 National Broadband Plan. The FCC established the 5G Fund in 2020, making available up to $9 billion in Universal Service Fund support over 10 years for mobile service in high-cost areas.

The existing rules require fund recipients to deliver conventional 5G speeds that today’s satellite service cannot yet provide. But before committing to a decade of conventional construction, the agency should create a direct-to-device tier to buy basic mobile coverage in places that towers cannot economically reach, then let competing terrestrial-satellite partnerships bid to provide it.

Instead of prescribing the infrastructure carriers must build, the FCC should buy the coverage it wants and let providers compete over how best to deliver it. How would it work? The FCC could ask carriers to bid for the minimum subsidy they need to provide satellite coverage in designated unserved areas without charging the premium. Carriers would receive support only in return for meeting clear requirements for availability, reliability, emergency communications and compatibility with widely used handsets.

That condition would advance the Communications Act’s promise that consumers in rural and high-cost areas should have access to communications services that are “reasonably comparable” to those available in urban areas, at “reasonably comparable” rates.

“Reasonably comparable” doesn’t require identical service or prices. Courts allow the FCC to balance comparability with affordability and responsible stewardship of the Universal Service Fund.

Here, the balance is clear. Spending enormous sums to extend a terrestrial network over the most challenging terrain would drain resources from places where towers remain economically viable. Leaving that terrain uncovered, on the other hand, perpetuates the rural divide. And charging those who most often encounter dead zones an additional $120 a year makes those least well served pay extra for basic connectivity.

The FCC’s rules require recipients of 5G Fund support to offer rural service at rates reasonably comparable to urban rates. Offering the same rates, terms and conditions in urban and rural areas can satisfy that rule. So, extending the requirement to subsidized direct-to-device coverage would be an evolution of existing universal-service policy, not a new system of price regulation.

Universal-service policy has always adapted to changes in network technology and economics. direct-to-device changes both. The last cell tower needed to close the rural divide no longer has to be built on the side of a mountain. It can be deployed in space, using a federal fund already authorized to bring mobile service to remote locations the market cannot economically reach.

Blair Levin is a former chief of staff of the Federal Communications Commission and directed the writing of the 2010 National Broadband Plan. Larry Downes is the co-author of “Big Bang Disruption” and other books on disruptive innovation.

data.title: Live updates: Trump leans into Ramaswamy ad controversy, heads to Florida rally
data.description:
President Trump will rally voters closer to home Friday afternoon, with a campaign stop in Fort Myers, Fla., as long-awaited midterm elections approach. He’ll be there to boost Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.), who’s running for governor, and Sen. Ashley Moody (R-Fla.), who is running for a full Senate term.

The president both Thursday night and Friday leaned further into the controversy surrounding Ohio GOP gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy’s advertisement.

The ad, which emerged late Monday, features Democrat Amy Acton’s mother claiming she is a “liar.” It has drawn fierce opposition from Democrats and some Republicans. But Trump and Vice President Vance are among those defending the video.

“So I told him, ‘Leave it up and look upstairs and say, “Thank you God, very much, I appreciate it,'” Trump said Thursday that he’d told Ramaswamy. “I only wish I could’ve had an ad like that against somebody.”

With 11 days until Election Day, the Justice Department preemptively sued to block certification of the Senate election in Alaska if incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses his reelection bid. 

And, Attorney General Todd Blanche did not dismiss the notion that the Department of Justice would intervene in states’ election verification processes, telling reporters Thursday there are hypothetical “scenarios” in which it could block the certification of votes.

Follow along live today.

data.title: Feds knocking on doors to question voters' immigration status: CBS
data.description:
We have officially moved into voter intimidation territory.   

According to a new CBS News investigation, armed, uniformed Department of Homeland Security agents are going door to door in several states, questioning residents about their immigration status and whether they’ve registered to vote or cast ballots.  

The administration says it’s targeting potential noncitizen voting. But noncitizens are already prohibited by law from voting in federal elections, and the evidence of widespread voter fraud simply isn’t there.  

One Brennan Center study examining 23.5 million votes across 42 jurisdictions identified just 30 suspected cases of voter fraud. That’s roughly one for every million votes.  

So why are federal agents knocking on people’s doors over an issue that the available evidence suggests is exceedingly rare?  

A federal judge was likely confused as well, since they ruled Wednesday that these operations likely violate the Voting Rights Act and ordered restrictions on the practice in nine states under specified circumstances. The judge also warned of a high likelihood of error in the government’s process for identifying potential targets.  

Let’s talk about all the errors that could be made here. A U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services whistleblower reported that employees were expected to review 40 people a day, spending roughly 12 minutes per person. How thoroughly can tens of thousands of records be vetted at that pace, particularly when American citizens are included in the data? Naturally, legal voters are going to get caught in the crossfire of this mess.  

Rep. Bennie G. Thompson, the top Democrat on the House Homeland Security Committee, called the operation a “anti-democratic departure from the mission Congress set for the Department” and described it as a “law enforcement activity aimed at intimidating the public as the 2026 midterm elections are underway.”  

I completely understand that concern. Imagine being a naturalized citizen, watching armed federal agents question your neighbors about voting. Even if you’re legally eligible to vote, you might wonder whether casting a ballot could put you or your family under scrutiny. That fear alone can keep people away from the polls.  

And remember, former Trump adviser Steve Bannon said earlier this year: “You’re damn right we’re gonna have ICE surround the polls come November. We’re not gonna sit here and allow you to steal the country again.”  

Sending ICE or any other armed federal agents to the polls is illegal, because federal law bans federal officers from interfering in elections. It’s also illegal because federal law bans troops and armed federal agents from being deployed anywhere an “election is held.”   

Bannon’s rhetoric, combined with door-to-door investigations and recent scrutiny and investigations of voter-registration groups, is feeling like voter intimidation.  

We’ve seen President Trump challenge the 2020 election results, including pressuring Georgia officials to “find votes.” Now, with the midterms approaching, voters are watching federal agencies expand their efforts to investigate alleged election fraud. Something we know is extremely rare. Claims of widespread voter fraud are unsupported by evidence and are being used to erode public confidence in elections.  

We need to protect eligible Americans’ right to vote without fear. If the administration believes it can win voters over, the answer is policy and persuasion, not tactics that risk making people afraid to exercise their fundamental right.  

Lindsey Granger is a NewsNation contributor and co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising.” This column is an edited transcription of her on-air commentary.
